lessons.title: IF: making decisions
learn: Pass or fail, bonus or no bonus
Text, numbers and blanks as results

steps.say: This is the sales team sheet we'll finish in this lesson. Every person gets a status, a bonus if they hit target, and a follow-up note only when one is needed. You'll use checks like this every month for incentive payouts.
Here's what you'll learn, using the practice sheet S04-01.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Write an IF formula that returns text
• Return a number, such as a bonus amount
• Return a blank cell when nothing is needed
Practice sheet: S04-01

steps.say: IF asks one question. If the answer is yes, it returns the first value, otherwise the second. The question is called the logical test, and it usually compares two things, such as sales and target.

acts.t:
IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false)
logical_test: a yes or no question, like E2>=D2
value_if_true: what to show when the answer is yes
value_if_false: what to show when the answer is no
Text results go inside double quotes

steps.say: Go to the practice sheet S04-01. Column D has each person's target and column E has actual sales. Click cell F2, where we'll write Aarav's status.
Type equals IF, open bracket. The test is E2 greater than or equal to D2, which reads: did sales reach the target? Then type a comma.
Next is the value if true. Type Achieved inside double quotes, then a comma. Text always needs quotes inside a formula.
Last, the value if false: Missed, also in quotes. Close the bracket and press Return. Aarav sold five lakh sixty-two thousand rupees against a target of five lakh, so he shows Achieved.
To copy it down, select F2 to F11 and press Command D to fill down. Look at Sneha in row 5. Her sales exactly equal her target, and because we used greater than or equal to, she counts as Achieved.

acts.h: Select F2:F11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: IF can return numbers too. In G2, the bonus is two percent of sales when the target is met, and zero otherwise. Type equals IF, E2 greater than or equal to D2, comma, E2 times 2 percent, comma, 0, close bracket, and press Return.
Fill it down with Command D. Aarav earns a bonus of eleven thousand two hundred and forty rupees, and everyone who missed target shows zero.

acts.h: Select G2:G11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Sometimes the right answer is nothing at all. In H2, if sales are below target, show Call manager. Otherwise type two double quotes with nothing between them. That returns an empty-looking cell, so the sheet stays clean.

acts.h: Type =IF(E2<D2,"Call manager","") and press Return

steps.say: Fill down. Only Priya, Imran, Arjun and Sourav get a follow-up note. Sourav missed by just one thousand rupees, and IF treats that exactly like a big miss.

acts.h: Select H2:H11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Here's the most common mistake. Retype F2 without the quotes around Achieved and Missed, and press Return. Excel shows the NAME error, because it thinks Achieved is the name of something it should already know.
Type the formula again with the quotes in place and press Return. The status is back. Whenever you see NAME after writing text in a formula, check your quotes first.

Now prove the sheet is live. Priya's sales figure was updated to four lakh sixty thousand. Click E3, type 460000 and press Return. Her status flips to Achieved, a bonus of nine thousand two hundred appears, and the follow-up note disappears.
Here's a quick recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• IF(test, value if true, value if false) makes one decision per row
• Results can be text in quotes, a number or a calculation
• Two double quotes "" return a blank-looking cell

steps.say: Your turn. In column I, show the word Star when sales are at least one hundred and twenty percent of target, and leave the cell blank otherwise. The answer is on the S04-01 Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
In I2:I11, show Star when sales are at least 120% of target, otherwise blank.
Hint: compare E2 with D2*1.2
Answer: sheet S04-01 Done

steps.say: This sheet decides who gets the quarterly incentive. HR's rule has two conditions, a second rule has an either-or condition, and the pay type depends on what someone is not. We'll build all of it with AND, OR and NOT.
Here's the plan for this lesson.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Test several conditions in one formula
• AND, OR and NOT return TRUE or FALSE
• Put them inside IF to get words in your report
Practice sheet: S04-02

steps.say: AND is TRUE only when every test passes. OR is TRUE when at least one test passes. NOT simply flips TRUE to FALSE and FALSE to TRUE.

acts.t:
AND(test1, test2, ...)  TRUE only if all tests are TRUE
OR(test1, test2, ...)  TRUE if any test is TRUE
NOT(test)  reverses TRUE and FALSE
Use them as the logical test inside IF

steps.say: Open sheet S04-02. Each row has a rating out of 5, attendance and years of tenure. The incentive rule is a rating of 4 or more and attendance of at least 90 percent. Click F2.
Type equals AND, open bracket. The first test is C2 greater than or equal to 4, then a comma.

The second test is D2 greater than or equal to 90 percent. You can type the percent sign straight into a formula. Close the bracket and press Return. Neha has a rating of 5 and 96 percent attendance, so AND gives TRUE.
Fill down with Command D. Vikram has a rating of 4 but only 88 percent attendance, so he gets FALSE. With AND, one failed test makes the whole answer FALSE.

acts.h: Select F2:F11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: OR is more relaxed. In G2, type equals OR, open bracket, C2 equals 5, comma, E2 greater than or equal to 5, close bracket, and press Return. It's TRUE for a top rating or for five years of service.
Fill down. Vikram is TRUE here because of his six years, even with a rating of 4. Ayesha, Rahul and Karan pass neither test, so they show FALSE.

acts.h: Select G2:G11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: TRUE and FALSE are fine for checking, but a report needs words. In H2, type equals IF, open bracket, and use the same AND test as the logical test, followed by a comma.
Then Eligible and Not eligible, each in quotes. Close the bracket and press Return.
Fill down. Five people are eligible: Neha, Rahul, Lakshmi, Siddharth and Harsh.

acts.h: Select H2:H11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: NOT flips a test. Sales staff earn commission and everyone else gets fixed pay. In I2, type equals IF, NOT of B2 equals Sales, then Fixed pay and Commission in quotes, and press Return.
Fill down. Every department other than Sales now shows Fixed pay.

acts.h: Select I2:I11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: A very common mistake is typing 90 instead of 90 percent. Retype F2 with D2 greater than or equal to 90, and press Return. Neha now shows FALSE, because attendance is stored as 0.96 and that is never 90 or more.
Put the percent sign back and press Return. Neha is TRUE again. When a cell shows a percentage, the value underneath is a decimal.
Now change an input. Vikram's attendance was corrected to 92 percent. Click D3, type 92 percent and press Return. His AND result turns TRUE and the incentive column says Eligible.
Here's a quick recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• AND needs every test to pass; OR needs just one
• NOT reverses a test, handy for 'everyone except'
• Put AND, OR or NOT inside IF to return words

steps.say: Your turn. In column J, show Needs review when the rating is 2 or less, or attendance is below 85 percent. Otherwise show OK. The answer is on the Done sheet.

acts.t:
Challenge
In J2:J11, show "Needs review" if rating <= 2 OR attendance < 85%, otherwise "OK".
Answer: sheet S04-02 Done

lessons.title: Nested IF, IFS and SWITCH
learn: When to use a lookup table instead

steps.say: Here are appraisal grades worked out three different ways, plus region names from short codes. By the end you'll know which method to pick, and when a small lookup table beats all of them.
Here's the plan for this lesson.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Grade bands with a nested IF
• The same bands with IFS
• Exact matches with SWITCH
• Bands from a lookup table
Practice sheet: S04-03

steps.say: A nested IF puts one IF inside another. IFS lists test and result pairs in order. SWITCH compares one value with a list of exact matches.

acts.t:
IF(B2>=90,"A+",IF(B2>=75,"A", ... ))
IFS(test1, result1, test2, result2, ..., TRUE, default)
SWITCH(value, match1, result1, match2, result2, ..., default)
IFS and SWITCH stop at the first match

steps.say: Open sheet S04-03. The bands are: 90 and above is A plus, 75 is A, 60 is B, 40 is C and anything lower is D. The same cut-offs are in the small table in J1 to K6.
In D2, start with the highest band. Type equals IF, open bracket, B2 greater than or equal to 90, comma, A plus in quotes, comma.
For the false part, start a second IF: B2 greater than or equal to 75 gives A. The first test has already failed, so this only catches scores from 75 to 89.
Add two more IFs for B and C, with D as the last fallback. Then close four brackets, one for each IF, and press Return.
Fill down with Command D. Anil with 92 gets A plus and Deepa with 35 gets D. It works, but four closing brackets are easy to get wrong.

acts.h: Select D2:D11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: IFS removes the nesting. In E2, list each test and its result in pairs: 90 and A plus, 75 and A, 60 and B, 40 and C. Press Return.
Fill down and look at Deepa in row 5. She shows the N A error, because her score of 35 matched none of the tests. IFS has no automatic otherwise.

acts.h: Select E2:E11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Fix it with one last pair: TRUE, then D in quotes. TRUE always passes, so it catches every score that's left over. Retype E2 and press Return.
Fill down again. Deepa now shows D, and column E matches column D exactly.

acts.h: Select E2:E11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: SWITCH is for exact matches, not ranges. In F2, switch on the code in C2: N gives North, S gives South, E gives East, W gives West, and anything else gives Unknown.
Fill down. Every code now has a full region name, and the formula is much shorter than four nested IFs.

acts.h: Select F2:F11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: When cut-offs change often, keep them in a table. In G2, XLOOKUP looks for the score in the Min score column and returns the grade. The minus one at the end means: if there's no exact match, take the next smaller value. The dollar signs lock the table.
Fill down. Same grades as before. We cover XLOOKUP fully in the lookup section.

acts.h: Select G2:G11 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Here's why the table wins. HR lowers the B cut-off from 60 to 55. Type 55 in J4 and press Return. Gauri's grade in column G moves from C to B at once, while columns D and E still say C, because their cut-offs are typed inside the formulas.
Here's a quick recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• Nested IF works but gets hard to read past three levels
• IFS is flatter; end it with TRUE, default
• SWITCH handles exact codes; a lookup table is best when bands change

steps.say: Your turn. In column H, use SWITCH on the grade in column D to return a bonus percentage: twenty percent for A plus, fifteen for A, ten for B and zero for anything else.

acts.t:
Challenge
In H2:H11, use SWITCH on D2: A+ gives 20%, A gives 15%, B gives 10%, otherwise 0.
Answer: sheet S04-03 Done

lessons.title: IFERROR, IFNA and the IS functions

steps.say: This vendor sheet had error codes all over it. In the finished version, every problem row shows a clear message, and a set of TRUE and FALSE checks tells you exactly what's wrong with each row.
Here's the plan for this lesson.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• Replace errors with a useful message, not a fake zero
• IFNA for lookups that find nothing
• ISBLANK, ISNUMBER, ISTEXT and ISERROR checks
Practice sheet: S04-04

steps.say: IFERROR catches any error. IFNA catches only the not-found error from lookups. The IS functions don't fix anything: they answer TRUE or FALSE about a value.

acts.t:
IFERROR(value, value_if_error)
IFNA(value, value_if_na)  only catches #N/A
ISBLANK(value)  ISNUMBER(value)
ISTEXT(value)  ISERROR(value)
Each IS function returns TRUE or FALSE

steps.say: Open sheet S04-04. This is a typical import: one quantity is zero, one is missing, one amount came in as text and one GST code isn't in our rate table on the right. Click D2 for the rate per unit.
Type equals B2 divided by C2, press Return, then fill down to D9 with Command D. Rows 3 and 6 show the DIV by zero error. Patel Packaging has zero quantity and Deccan Steel has none.

acts.h: Select D2:D9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: A quick fix many people use is IFERROR with zero. Retype D2 as equals IFERROR, open bracket, B2 divided by C2, comma, 0, close bracket, and fill down. The errors are gone, but a rate of zero now looks like real data.

acts.h: Select D2:D9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: A better habit is to return a message that says what to fix. Change the second argument to Check qty in quotes and fill down again. The sheet is clean and the problem rows still stand out.

acts.h: Type =IFERROR(B2/C2,"Check qty") and press Return
Select D2:D9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Now the GST rate. In F2, type equals IFNA, open bracket. Inside it, XLOOKUP finds the code from E2 in the code column L and returns the rate from column M. The dollar signs lock the table. Then a comma.

Finish with Code missing in quotes, close the bracket and press Return, then fill down. Annapurna Caterers uses GST12, which isn't in our table, so it shows Code missing. Any other kind of error would still show, which is what you want.

acts.h: Type "Code missing") and press Return
Select F2:F9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: The IS functions answer questions about a cell. In G2, type equals ISBLANK of C2, press Return and fill down. Only Deccan Steel's quantity is empty, so only row 6 is TRUE.

acts.h: Select G2:G9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: In H2, ISNUMBER of B2 checks the amount. Fill down. Lotus Office Supplies shows FALSE: its amount came in as text. The division still worked, but SUM would quietly skip that row.

acts.h: Select H2:H9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: ISERROR is TRUE for any error at all. In I2, type equals ISERROR of B2 divided by C2 and fill down. It flags exactly the two rows that IFERROR is covering in column D.

acts.h: Select I2:I9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Fix the data and the messages clear on their own. Patel Packaging actually bought 140 units. Type 140 in C3 and press Return. The rate becomes ninety rupees and the error check for row 3 turns FALSE.
Here's a quick recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• IFERROR with a message, not 0, so problems stay visible
• IFNA only hides 'not found', so other errors still show
• IS functions return TRUE or FALSE for checks and flags

steps.say: Your turn. In column J, use ISTEXT to flag amounts that are stored as text. Only one row should be TRUE.

acts.t:
Challenge
In J2:J9, use ISTEXT on column B to flag amounts stored as text.
Answer: sheet S04-04 Done

lessons.title: COUNTIF and COUNTIFS
learn: Count by region, status and date range
Wildcards and comparison operators in criteria

steps.say: Every answer in column I counts orders that meet a condition: by region, by status, above an amount, inside a date range, or by a name pattern. These are the questions your manager asks on a Monday morning.
Here's the plan for this lesson.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• COUNTIF for one condition, COUNTIFS for several
• Comparison operators: >, <, >=, <=, <>
• Wildcards: * for any characters
• Criteria that read a cell or a date
Practice sheet: S04-05

steps.say: COUNTIF takes a range and a condition. COUNTIFS takes pairs of range and condition, and counts rows where every pair is true.

acts.t:
COUNTIF(range, criteria)
COUNTIFS(range1, criteria1, range2, criteria2, ...)
Criteria examples:
"North"   ">50000"   ">"&I10   "A*"   "<>Cancelled"

steps.say: Open sheet S04-05. There are twenty orders from April to June 2026. The questions are in column H and the answers go in column I. Click I2.
Type equals COUNTIF, open bracket. The range is the Region column, C2 to C21. After a comma, the criteria is North in quotes. Close the bracket and press Return. Seven orders came from North.
Same idea in I3 for status: COUNTIF of E2 to E21, with Pending in quotes. Eight orders are still pending.
For two conditions, use COUNTIFS. In I4, type equals COUNTIFS, open bracket, then the first pair: the Region range, C2 to C21, and North.
Then the second pair: the Status range, E2 to E21, and Delivered. Close the bracket and press Return. Both must be true, so only four orders count.

Next, orders above the threshold in I10, which is fifty thousand rupees. A natural guess is to put greater than I10 inside the quotes. Type it in I5 and press Return. The answer is zero, which is clearly wrong.
Inside quotes, I10 is just text. Keep only the greater-than sign in quotes, then type an ampersand and I10 outside the quotes. Excel joins the sign with the value, and the answer becomes thirteen.
Dates work the same way. In I6, type equals COUNTIFS, open bracket, the Date column, and greater than or equal to, joined with DATE of 2026, 5, 1. DATE builds a date from a year, month and day.
The second pair uses the same Date column again, with less than or equal to the thirty-first of May. Close the bracket and press Return. Eight orders fall in May.
Wildcards help with text. The star means any characters. In I7, COUNTIF of the Salesperson column with A star counts every name that starts with A, so Amit and Anjali together give nine.
Now change the threshold in I10 to one lakh. Type 100000 and press Return. The count in I5 drops to four, because the formula reads the cell instead of a number typed into it.
Here's a quick recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• COUNTIF for one condition, COUNTIFS for many, all must be true
• Operators go in quotes; join cell values with &
• * matches any characters, and dates use ">="&DATE(...)

steps.say: Your turn. In I8, count South orders that were not cancelled. Use the not-equal sign, which is a less-than sign followed by a greater-than sign.

acts.t:
Challenge
In I8, count South orders whose status is not Cancelled.
Hint: "<>Cancelled"
Answer: sheet S04-05 Done

lessons.title: SUMIF, SUMIFS, AVERAGEIFS, MAXIFS, MINIFS
learn: A region-by-month summary from raw sales
Criteria from cells, not typed text

steps.say: From thirty raw sales rows, we'll build a region-by-month summary with one formula, plus a small panel where you type a region and get its total, average, largest and smallest sale.
Here's the plan for this lesson.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• SUMIFS for a region-by-month grid
• Criteria taken from cells, not typed text
• SUMIF, AVERAGEIFS, MAXIFS and MINIFS
Practice sheet: S04-06

steps.say: SUMIFS starts with the range to add, then pairs of range and condition. AVERAGEIFS, MAXIFS and MINIFS use the same order. The older SUMIF is different: its range to add comes last.

acts.t:
SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, ...)
AVERAGEIFS / MAXIFS / MINIFS: same order as SUMIFS
SUMIF(range, criteria, [sum_range])  sum range LAST

steps.say: Open sheet S04-06. These are sales from April to June 2026, the first quarter of FY 2026-27. Regions run down column G and months across row 1. Select H2 to J5, all twelve cells of the grid.
Type equals SUMIFS, open bracket. The first argument is what to add: the Amount column, D2 to D31, with dollar signs so it never moves.
Next, the Region column, locked, and the condition: G2, the region name in the grid. Put the dollar only before G, so every column of the grid keeps reading column G.
Then the Month column and its condition, H1. This time the dollar goes before the 1, so every row keeps reading the month headings in row 1. Close the bracket.
Now press Control Return instead of Return. The formula goes into all twelve selected cells, and each one adjusts to its own region and month.
Check a couple of answers. South in May is sixty-six thousand rupees. East shows zero for April, because East made no sales that month. That's a correct answer, not an error.

Now a total per region in K2. A common slip is using the SUMIFS order with SUMIF: amounts first, then regions. Type it and press Return. The answer is zero, because SUMIF expects the range to add last.
Retype it in the right order: the Region column, then G2, then the Amount column. Press Return and fill down to K5.

acts.h: Select K2:K5 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Now the panel below. H8 holds the region we want, South. In H9, type equals SUMIF of B2 to B31, H8, and D2 to D31. The criteria comes from a cell, so you never edit the formula.
In H10, AVERAGEIFS uses the SUMIFS order: the Amount column first, then the Region column and H8. The average South sale is thirty-seven thousand five hundred rupees.

MAXIFS and MINIFS follow the same pattern. Type MAXIFS in H11 and MINIFS in H12 with the same three arguments. The largest South sale is sixty thousand five hundred and the smallest is nineteen thousand five hundred.
Now type North in H8 and press Return. All four answers switch to North at once. North's total is five lakh sixty-three thousand rupees. This is why criteria belong in cells.
Here's a quick recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• SUMIFS, AVERAGEIFS, MAXIFS, MINIFS: the result range comes first
• SUMIF: the range to add comes last
• Use $G2 and H$1 so one formula fills a whole grid

steps.say: Your turn. In H13, find the average West sale in June with AVERAGEIFS and two conditions.

acts.t:
Challenge
In H13, average West sales in June using AVERAGEIFS with two conditions (Region and Month).
Answer: sheet S04-06 Done

steps.say: These results come from one function, SUMPRODUCT: total revenue without a helper column, a weighted average price and North's revenue only. You'll also see the TRUE and FALSE trick that makes conditional maths work.
Here's the plan for this lesson.

acts.t:
In this lesson
• SUMPRODUCT: multiply row by row, then add
• Weighted averages
• TRUE = 1 and FALSE = 0 for conditional sums
Practice sheet: S04-07

steps.say: SUMPRODUCT multiplies matching items in two or more ranges and adds the results. All ranges must be the same size.

acts.t:
SUMPRODUCT(array1, [array2], ...)
Row by row: array1 x array2, then add them all
In maths, TRUE counts as 1 and FALSE as 0
(B2:B13="North")*C2:C13 keeps only North rows

steps.say: Open sheet S04-07. Each row has a product, region, quantity sold and price per unit. Click G2 for total revenue.

Type equals SUMPRODUCT, open bracket, C2 to C13, comma, D2 to D13, close bracket, and press Return. Excel multiplies each quantity by its price and adds the twelve results. Total revenue is two lakh eighty-six thousand four hundred and fifty-one rupees.
In G3, a plain AVERAGE of the prices gives about one thousand two hundred and sixteen rupees. That's misleading, because we sold eight chairs but a hundred and twenty reams of paper.

A weighted average gives each price a weight equal to its quantity. In G4, type the same SUMPRODUCT and divide it by the SUM of C2 to C13. The real average price per unit sold is about four hundred and seventy-six rupees.
Now the trick behind conditional maths. In G6, type equals B2 equals North in quotes, and press Return. Excel answers TRUE, because row 2 is North.
In G7, put that test in brackets and multiply it by 1. TRUE becomes 1, and FALSE would become 0. So multiplying by a test keeps the rows that pass and turns the rest into zero.
Use this in G5 for North revenue. Type equals SUMPRODUCT, open bracket, and in brackets, B2 to B13 equals North. That gives twelve TRUE or FALSE answers, one per row.

Multiply by the quantities and the prices, close the bracket and press Return. Rows from other regions become zero, so the answer is North only: one lakh forty-three thousand one hundred and sixty-five rupees.

A common mistake is ranges of different sizes. Retype G2 with D2 to D12, one row short, and press Return. You get the VALUE error, because SUMPRODUCT needs every range to have the same number of rows.
Fix the range back to D13 and press Return. The total is back.
Now change an input. The stapler order in row 3 was actually for North. Type North in B3 and press Return. North revenue rises by seven thousand two hundred rupees, the value of that order.
Here's a quick recap.

acts.t:
Recap
• SUMPRODUCT multiplies row by row and adds, no helper column
• Weighted average = SUMPRODUCT(qty, price) / SUM(qty)
• Multiply by (test) to keep only the rows that pass

steps.say: Your turn. In G8, find North revenue only from rows where the quantity is 50 or more. Multiply by two tests.

acts.t:
Challenge
In G8: North revenue where quantity is 50 or more.
Hint: (B2:B13="North")*(C2:C13>=50)*C2:C13*D2:D13
Answer: sheet S04-07 Done

lessons.title: Project: income tax calculator (new regime)
learn: Slab-based tax with a lookup table

steps.say: This is a new regime income tax calculator for financial year 2025-26, the year that ended on thirty-first March 2026. Type a gross salary and it works out taxable income, slab tax, the section 87A rebate, cess and the monthly TDS.
Here's what this project covers.

acts.t:
In this project
• Slab tax from a table, using MAX and MIN
• Standard deduction of ₹75,000
• Section 87A rebate up to ₹12 lakh taxable income, with marginal relief
• 4% health and education cess
Practice sheet: S04-08

steps.say: Here are the new regime slabs for financial year 2025-26, assessment year 2026-27. Salaried people also get a standard deduction of seventy-five thousand rupees, and the 87A rebate makes the tax zero when taxable income is up to twelve lakh rupees.

acts.t:
New regime, FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27)
Up to ₹4 lakh: nil
₹4 to 8 lakh: 5%
₹8 to 12 lakh: 10%
₹12 to 16 lakh: 15%
₹16 to 20 lakh: 20%
₹20 to 24 lakh: 25%
Above ₹24 lakh: 30%
Standard deduction ₹75,000. Cess 4% on the tax.

steps.say: Open sheet S04-08. The inputs are on the left: Neha's gross salary of sixteen lakh fifty thousand rupees and the standard deduction. The slab table is on the right. Click B6.

Taxable income is gross salary minus the standard deduction. Type equals MAX, open bracket, B4 minus B5, comma, zero, and press Return. MAX with zero means a tiny salary never gives a negative number. Taxable income is fifteen lakh seventy-five thousand rupees.
Now the slab table. For each slab we need the part of the income that falls inside it: the smaller of taxable income and the slab's upper limit, minus the slab's lower limit. Click G3.
Type equals, open bracket, MIN of dollar B dollar 6 and E3, close bracket, minus D3, close bracket, times F3, and press Return. The dollar signs keep every row pointing at the taxable income in B6.

Fill down to G9 with Command D. The first four rows look right, but the twenty, twenty-five and thirty percent rows are negative. Neha's income never reaches those slabs, so the subtraction drops below zero.

acts.h: Select G3:G9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Wrap the income part in MAX with zero. Retype G3 as equals MAX, open bracket, zero, comma, MIN of B6 and E3 minus D3, close bracket, times F3. Fill down again. Unused slabs now show zero.

acts.h: Select G3:G9 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Read the column: twenty thousand from the five percent slab, forty thousand from the ten percent slab, and fifty-six thousand two hundred and fifty from the fifteen percent slab. In B7, type equals SUM of G3 to G9. Tax on slabs is one lakh sixteen thousand two hundred and fifty rupees.

The rebate has two parts. Up to twelve lakh of taxable income, the whole tax is rebated. Just above twelve lakh, marginal relief applies: the tax can't be more than the income that crosses twelve lakh.

acts.t:
Section 87A rebate, new regime, FY 2025-26
Taxable income up to ₹12,00,000: rebate = the full tax (at most ₹60,000)
Just above ₹12 lakh: marginal relief, so tax can't exceed the income above ₹12 lakh

steps.say: In B8, type equals IF, open bracket, B6 less than or equal to 1200000, comma, B7, comma. So at or below twelve lakh, the rebate is the whole tax.

Otherwise the rebate is the tax minus the income above twelve lakh, never below zero. Type MAX of B7 minus, in brackets, B6 minus 1200000, comma, zero. Close both brackets and press Return. Neha is well above the limit, so her rebate is zero.
In B9, tax after rebate is B7 minus B8. In B10, the cess is four percent of that, rounded to whole rupees with ROUND, comma, zero.
In B11, total tax is tax plus cess: one lakh twenty thousand nine hundred rupees. In B12, divide by 12 and round, for a monthly TDS of ten thousand and seventy-five rupees.

Now test the rebate. Change the gross salary in B4 to twelve lakh seventy-five thousand. Taxable income is exactly twelve lakh, slab tax is sixty thousand, the rebate cancels all of it, and total tax is zero.

Now try thirteen lakh. Taxable income is twelve lakh twenty-five thousand and slab tax is sixty-three thousand seven hundred and fifty. Marginal relief limits the tax to the twenty-five thousand rupees above twelve lakh, so the rebate is thirty-eight thousand seven hundred and fifty. With cess, the total is twenty-six thousand rupees.

Keep the assumptions in mind. This sheet is for a resident individual with salary income under the new regime, below fifty lakh so there's no surcharge. Special-rate income such as capital gains follows its own rules.

acts.t:
Assumptions
• FY 2025-26 (AY 2026-27), new regime, resident individual
• Salary income only, total under ₹50 lakh (no surcharge)
• Special-rate income such as capital gains has its own rules

• 87A rebate with IF, plus marginal relief just above ₹12 lakh
